```{r setup, include = FALSE}
  collapse = TRUE,
  comment = "#>",

library(multinma)
library(mid.nma.rank)
library(dplyr)

options(mc.cores = parallel::detectCores())
```

## Introduction

This vignette demonstrates how to apply MID-adjusted treatment ranking
methods to a multilevel network meta-regression (ML-NMR) analysis, and is an 
adaptation of the associated **multinma** vignette available at:
https://dmphillippo.github.io/multinma/articles/example_plaque_psoriasis.html

The example uses the plaque psoriasis datasets supplied with
**multinma**, consisting of a mixture of individual participant data
(IPD) and aggregate data (AgD) studies. We fit an ML-NMR model,
calculate conventional treatment rankings, and then re-rank treatments
using a clinically motivated minimally important difference (MID).
This exact example was published in the Curteis et al.(2026) ISPOR EU poster.
[@curteis2026ranking] For details on the methodology emplyed, see Curteis
et al. (2025).[@curteis2025ranking]

## Data preparation

The plaque psoriasis example combines IPD and AgD studies.

```{r data}
data(plaque_psoriasis_ipd)
data(plaque_psoriasis_agd)

pso_ipd <- plaque_psoriasis_ipd
pso_agd <- plaque_psoriasis_agd
```

The IPD data require several covariate transformations and a treatment
classification variable.

```{r data-ipd}
pso_ipd <- plaque_psoriasis_ipd %>%
  mutate(
    bsa = bsa / 100,
    weight = weight / 10,
    durnpso = durnpso / 10,
    prevsys = as.numeric(prevsys),
    psa = as.numeric(psa),

    trtclass = case_when(
      trtn == 1 ~ "Placebo",
      trtn %in% c(2, 3, 5, 6) ~ "IL-17 blocker",
      trtn == 4 ~ "TNFa blocker",
      trtn == 7 ~ "IL-12/23 blocker"
    ),

    is_complete = complete.cases(
      durnpso,
      prevsys,
      bsa,
      weight,
      psa
    )
  ) %>%
  arrange(studyc, trtn)
```

Equivalent transformations are applied to the aggregate data.

```{r data-agd}
pso_agd <- plaque_psoriasis_agd %>%
  mutate(
    bsa_mean = bsa_mean / 100,
    bsa_sd = bsa_sd / 100,
    weight_mean = weight_mean / 10,
    weight_sd = weight_sd / 10,
    durnpso_mean = durnpso_mean / 10,
    durnpso_sd = durnpso_sd / 10,
    prevsys = prevsys / 100,
    psa = psa / 100,

    trtclass = case_when(
      trtn == 1 ~ "Placebo",
      trtn %in% c(2, 3, 5, 6) ~ "IL-17 blocker",
      trtn == 4 ~ "TNFa blocker",
      trtn == 7 ~ "IL-12/23 blocker"
    )
  ) %>%
  arrange(studyc, trtn)
```

The proportion of missing covariate information in the IPD studies can
be summarised as follows.

```{r missing}
pso_ipd %>%
  group_by(studyc) %>%
  summarise(
    n_total = n(),
    n_missing = sum(!is_complete),
    pct_missing = mean(!is_complete) * 100
  )
```

For simplicity, patients with missing covariate information are removed.

```{r complete-cases}
pso_ipd <- filter(pso_ipd, is_complete)
```

## Network construction

The IPD and AgD studies are combined into a single network.

```{r network}
pso_net <- combine_network(
  set_ipd(
    pso_ipd,
    study = studyc,
    trt = trtc,
    r = pasi90,
    trt_class = trtclass
  ),
  set_agd_arm(
    pso_agd,
    study = studyc,
    trt = trtc,
    r = pasi90_r,
    n = pasi90_n,
    trt_class = trtclass
  )
)

pso_net
```

## ML-NMR integration model

Aggregate studies are integrated using numerical integration over the
covariate distributions reported within each study.

```{r integration}
pso_net <- add_integration(
  pso_net,
  durnpso = distr(
    qgamma,
    mean = durnpso_mean,
    sd = durnpso_sd
  ),
  prevsys = distr(
    qbern,
    prob = prevsys
  ),
  bsa = distr(
    qlogitnorm,
    mean = bsa_mean,
    sd = bsa_sd
  ),
  weight = distr(
    qgamma,
    mean = weight_mean,
    sd = weight_sd
  ),
  psa = distr(
    qbern,
    prob = psa
  ),
  n_int = 64
)
```

## Fitting the ML-NMR model

A fixed-effect ML-NMR model is fitted using a binomial likelihood and
logit link.

```{r fit, results="hide", warning=FALSE, message=FALSE}
pso_fit_FE <- nma(
  pso_net,
  trt_effects = "fixed",
  link = "logit",
  likelihood = "bernoulli2",
  regression =
    ~(durnpso + prevsys + bsa + weight + psa) * .trt,
  class_interactions = "common",
  prior_intercept = normal(scale = 10),
  prior_trt = normal(scale = 10),
  prior_reg = normal(scale = 10),
  init_r = 0.1,
  QR = TRUE
)
```

```{r fit-summary}
pso_fit_FE
```

## Model outputs

The fitted model can be explored through treatment effects and alternative metrics.

### Relative treatment effects

```{r releff}
pso_releff_FE <- relative_effects(pso_fit_FE)

forest_logit <- plot(
  pso_releff_FE,
  ref_line = 0
)

forest_logit
```

## Choosing the Minimally Important Difference (MID)

The MID must be defined on the same scale as the model's treatment
effects.

In this example we consider a clinically motivated MID inspired by the
IXORA-S study, which compared ixekizumab with ustekinumab in patients
with moderate-to-severe plaque psoriasis.[@reich2017comparison]

For illustration, suppose:

- the baseline PASI90 response probability was 43%;
- a 12.6% absolute increase in response was considered clinically
  important.

We convert this risk difference into the log-odds scale used by the
model.

```{r mid}
p1 <- 0.43
dp <- 0.126

p2 <- p1 + dp

logit <- function(p) {
  log(p / (1 - p))
}

mid <- logit(p2) - logit(p1)

mid
exp(mid)
```

The exponentiated value may be interpreted as the minimum odds ratio by
which one treatment must exceed another before it is considered superior
for ranking purposes.

## Rankings without an MID

For comparison, conventional rankings ignoring any MID are generated
as follows:

```{r rank-standard}
rank_0 <- posterior_ranks(
  pso_fit_FE,
  summary = TRUE,
  sucra = TRUE,
  lower_better = FALSE
)

rank_0
```

```{r rank-standard-plot}
plot(rank_0)
```

### Rank probabilities

```{r rank-probs-standard}
rank_probs <- posterior_rank_probs(
  pso_fit_FE,
  lower_better = FALSE
)

plot(rank_probs)
```

### Cumulative rank probabilities

```{r cumulative-standard}
rank_probs_cum <- posterior_rank_probs(
  pso_fit_FE,
  cumulative = TRUE,
  lower_better = FALSE
)

plot(rank_probs_cum)
```

## Rankings with an MID

MID-adjusted rankings are obtained using the functions provided by
**mid.nma.rank**.

```{r rank-mid}
rank_mid <- posterior_ranks_mid(
  pso_fit_FE,
  summary = TRUE,
  sucra = TRUE,
  mid = mid,
  lower_better = FALSE
)

rank_mid
```

```{r rank-mid-plot}
plot(rank_mid)
```

### Rank probabilities

Treatment rank probabilities can also be estimated while accounting for
the MID.

```{r probs-mid}
rank_probs_mid <- posterior_rank_probs_mid(
  pso_fit_FE,
  mid = mid,
  lower_better = FALSE
)

rank_probs_mid
```

```{r probs-mid-plot}
plot(rank_probs_mid)
```

Because treatments can be tied when differences do not exceed the MID,
intermediate ranks such as 1.5 or 2.5 may occur. The default midpoint
approach for handling ties preserves the desirable property that the
average SUCRA value across the network is 0.5.[@curteis2025ranking]

### Cumulative rank probabilities

Cumulative ranking probabilities can also be estimated while accounting for 
the MID.

```{r probs-cum-mid}
rank_probs_cum_mid <- posterior_rank_probs_mid(
  pso_fit_FE,
  cumulative = TRUE,
  mid = mid,
  lower_better = FALSE
)

plot(rank_probs_cum_mid)
```

## Interpretation

Conventional rankings treat any estimated treatment difference as
sufficient evidence for one treatment being superior to another.

MID-adjusted rankings instead require treatments to differ by a
clinically meaningful amount before one is ranked above the other. This
typically increases the probability of ties and can materially alter
rank probabilities, median ranks and SUCRA values. Consequently,
MID-adjusted rankings may better reflect clinically relevant differences
between treatments rather than purely statistical differences.
